Title: Functional substitution of imatinib-inactivated canonical oncoprotein BCR::ABL1 by overexpressed PLAG1 results in BCR::ABL1-independent resistance in blast phase of chronic myeloid leukemia.
Abstract: Inactivation of oncogenic BCR::ABL1 by imatinib in the early chronic phase (CP) of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) has achieved unprecedented clinical success, which eludes the majority of terminal blast crisis (BC) patients, predominantly due to the scantily understood BCR::ABL1-independent mechanism/s of resistance. Our earlier proteomic studies on K562 and KU812 cell lines, which mimicked the BCR::ABL1-independent resistance to imatinib reported in CML patients, demonstrated that atypical activation of signalling downstream of imatinib-inactivated BCR::ABL1, mediated by reduced levels of cell adhesion receptor - integrin ITGB1, caused resistance. In the present study, events upstream of ITGB1 were derived from the transcriptome, methylome, and miRNA profiles of imatinib-resistant cell lines. The analyses identified major alterations in cell adhesion pathway molecules in resistant cells. Significant among them were gene hypomethylation, upregulation of the transcript and protein of ITGB3, known to influence the protein level of ITGB1, which was reduced despite unaltered gene methylation and transcription. Indeed, knockdown (KD) of ITGB3 caused augmentation of ITGB1 protein level. Further, the mediator of ITGB3 overexpression was detected in genomic analysis. A recurrent gain at chromosomal region 8q11.21-12.1 and amplification of the transcription factor PLAG1 residing therein were observed in resistant K562 cells and CD34 + cells from resistant BC patients. KD of PLAG1 not only reversed gene hypomethylation, upregulation of transcript and protein of ITGB3 but also restored ITGB1 level and sensitized resistant cells to imatinib. The study has identified events upstream of ITGB1, thereby advancing the understanding of BCR::ABL1-independent imatinib resistance and has provided explorable therapeutic avenues for imatinib-resistant blast phase CML.

Title: Non-coding RNAs as mediators of tyrosine kinase inhibitor resistance in chronic myeloid leukemia: a scoping review.
Abstract: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) have transformed chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) from a life-threatening disease into a manageable chronic condition. However, 30-50% of patients require TKI switching due to resistance or intolerance, and BCR::ABL1-independent resistance mechanisms remain the most frequent and least understood cause. Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) - including microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), and circular RNAs (circRNAs) - have emerged as regulators of TKI resistance. This scoping review aimed to characterize the role of ncRNAs in TKI resistance, and to evaluate their potential as biomarkers and therapeutic targets. A systematic literature search was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE in April 2026, supplemented by manual reference searching. Of 374 identified records, 25 studies published between 2021 and 2025, plus one 2020 study identified through manual searching were included. miRNAs were the most frequently evaluated (64%), followed by lncRNAs (16%) and circRNAs (12%), with imatinib as the predominant TKI studied. Four axes were identified for miRNAs: downstream BCR::ABL1 signaling regulation, the miR-185/PAK6 axis, apoptosis and protective autophagy modulation, and drug efflux mechanisms. circRNAs and lncRNAs were found to act as competing endogenous RNAs regulating resistance via PI3K/AKT/mTOR, RAS/MAPK, and autophagy pathways. Prospective multicenter validation, particularly in countries with limited access to second- and third-generation TKIs, is a priority for future research.

Title: A Case of Duffy-Null-Associated Neutropenia in a Patient With Chronic Myeloid Leukemia.
Abstract: Duffy-null-associated neutrophil count (DANC) refers to a below-normal absolute neutrophil count (ANC < 1.5 × 10<sup>3</sup>/L), present most commonly in African American individuals. Neutropenia is a result of a lack of Fya and Fyb antigens on red blood cells. These patients do not have an increased risk of infection and may have an ANC < 1.5 × 10<sup>3</sup>/L at baseline. This unique case presents Duffy-null-associated neutropenia in the setting of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). A 64-year-old African American female presented to the emergency department on May 17, 2021, for fatigue and was found to have a white blood cell (WBC) count of 65.3 × 10<sup>9</sup>/L. Hematology and oncology referral led to a diagnosis of CML. Subsequently, she began treatment with imatinib (Gleevec) 400 mg daily. One month into treatment, she was neutropenic, with an ANC of 0.6 × 10<sup>3</sup>/L. For the next several years, this patient repeatedly had treatment holds and dose reductions in response to recurrent neutropenia. When BCR-ABL1 transcript level continued to increase, indicating poor treatment response, she was referred to Medical University of South Carolina (MUSC). After several treatment changes due to adverse effects, she began treatment with asciminib 80 mg daily. BCR-ABL1 transcript level with asciminib was consistently below 0.1%, indicating successful treatment response. Despite this milestone, she continued to have episodes of neutropenia, prompting a check for Duffy antigen presence. Testing confirmed the lack of Fya and Fyb antigens, indicating Duffy-null status. This case demonstrates the importance of identifying Duffy-null individuals. Despite achieving major molecular response, the patient had persistent neutropenia, leading to the investigation of Duffy-null status. It is hypothesized that underlying Duffy-null status may have caused neutropenia, rather than an adverse reaction to treatment. Early detection of Duffy-null status can prevent dose reductions in therapy and delayed remission. Particularly with African American patients, a better framework for addressing Duffy-null neutropenia may benefit long-term outcomes in the setting of cancer therapy.
